hypotheses.hypothesis: Coverage of democratic stakes and election-integrity disputes should rise as politics becomes more personally consequential, so importance should move toward 'Very important' (Direction B).
Pocketbook framing of politics, where economic hardship is discussed as separate from government, should grow as politics feels less relevant to daily life (Direction A).
Civic-duty language about voting should give way to futility language as the average respondent moves toward 'Not at all important' (Direction A).

Within coverage of foreign policy, language framing the issue as a personal or national cause should replace detached 'distant conflict' language as politics becomes more important to people (Direction B).
Voter-guide and candidate-forum activity, a concrete sign of active political preparation, should increase as people treat politics as very important (Direction B).
Coverage of elective care backlogs and deteriorating patient conditions rises as health worsens, so these phrases should become more common (Direction A).
Recovery and remission language increases as more people report feeling well (Direction B).
Cardiac and stroke reporting rises when self-rated health falls, since severe cardiovascular events signal worsening population health (Direction A).
Descriptions of people as frail or struggling give way to descriptions of vigour and recovery as self-rated health improves (Direction B).
Older-age coverage shifts from healthy, independent ageing toward care-system strain and frailty as self-rated health declines (Direction A).
Coverage increasingly reports that fewer Americans belong to a church, reflecting a shift toward nonmembership.

hypotheses.hypothesis: After the pandemic, coverage of in-person worship returning suggests more members re-engaged with congregations, moving the average toward active membership.
Descriptions shift from traditional parish life and Sunday worship toward secular identity and faith fading, indicating movement toward nonmembership.
Within charitable church activity, coverage moves from members who are largely absent to members actively staffing congregational outreach, indicating movement toward active membership.
Reports of congregations gaining formal members through joining processes indicate rising active membership.

Coverage of women's and girls' participation campaigns (named national drives and programmes) increases over time, reflecting more people being pulled into organised, registered playing rather than spectating.
In local sports reporting, coverage of clubs shutting down or failing to complete seasons becomes more frequent over time, pointing to a shift away from organised team membership.

Early coverage frames participants as spectators or casual observers, while later coverage frames them as registered players progressing through a club pathway, indicating movement toward active membership.

Within hockey and netball clubs, early reporting centres on playing members paying match fees, while later reporting centres on social or honorary members who no longer take the field, indicating movement toward non-membership in playing terms.
Coverage of youth and mini-football participation schemes grows over time, reflecting rising sign-ups for organised junior sessions and team registrations.
Coverage of former party members increases over time, reflecting a growing pool of people who say they are no longer members.
Coverage of party joining increases in the direction of active engagement: reports of new recruits and surging sign-ups rise over time.
Over time, descriptions of party supporters shift from active campaign workers toward formally unaffiliated or unenrolled voters, indicating movement toward non-membership.
In local party chapter coverage, passive support gives way over time to active roles, indicating a shift toward active membership.
Reports of people cancelling or failing to renew party dues rise over time, consistent with a move toward non-membership.
Coverage of humanitarian and charitable work increasingly describes hands-on, in-person service tasks, pointing to a shift toward active participation.
In community youth and civic groups, reports of members dropping out or opting out of the association increase, indicating movement toward non-membership.
Reporting shifts from purchase-style engagement such as galas and raffles toward sustained committee and team service roles, indicating more active membership.
Around food, toy, and blood drives, coverage moves from participants showing up to drives toward people explicitly sitting out or declining to take part, signaling movement toward non-membership.
Coverage increasingly reports people unsubscribing from or disconnecting from charitable organizations' communications and affiliations, reflecting a drift toward not being affiliated.

As acceptance of cross-racial intimacy grew, coverage of interracial dating and intermarriage should increase, pointing toward movement in Direction B (more people willing to have neighbors of another race).

Neighborhood-level suspicion of newcomers, expressed through watch-group and 'suspicious outsider' language, should rise in coverage if neighbors became more wary of people of other races, pointing toward Direction A.
Outdated racial terminology used in mainstream coverage should give way to 'people of color' and group-specific self-identification terms as public attitudes softened, pointing toward Direction B.

Rhetoric framing Asian residents as foreign threats shifted toward virus-blame language in the pandemic era, which should signal increased objection to neighbors of other races, pointing toward Direction A.
Colorblind and post-racial framing became more common in public discourse as explicit racial exclusion became less socially acceptable, indicating movement toward Direction B.
Coverage of parallel legal systems and religiously framed family disputes rises as opposition to religiously different neighbours hardens (direction A: more 'Mentioned').
Coverage of local street-level community gatherings rises as neighbours become more willing to live beside people of other faiths (direction B: more 'Not mentioned').
Public discussion shifts from framing religious minorities as a security or cultural problem to framing them through equal rights, which tracks increasing acceptance (direction B).
Reports of vandalism and harassment targeting Jewish sites and people increase as neighbourhood hostility grows (direction A: more 'Mentioned').
Debate over call-to-prayer and church-bell sound shifts from noise complaints and bans toward tolerance and heritage framing as neighbour acceptance improves (direction B).
Coverage of cohabitation increasingly reports demographic statistics and census counts, reflecting normalization of unmarried co-residence and a shift toward acceptance (Direction B).
Neighborhood-safety and crime-watch discourse increasingly frames unmarried residents as a conduct concern, consistent with more explicit objections to unmarried neighbors (Direction A).
Descriptions of unmarried living arrangements shift from moralized condemnation toward neutral, private-choice language, indicating movement toward acceptance (Direction B).
University and student-housing coverage increasingly addresses unmarried couples in coed or off-campus housing as routine policy matters, signaling greater tolerance (Direction B).

Condominium and HOA coverage shifts from framing unmarried residents as a threat to property standards toward framing them as a matter of lawful, equal occupancy, reflecting movement toward acceptance (Direction B).
If public suspicion of others rose, coverage of distinctive confidence-trick schemes aimed at ordinary people should increase in frequency.
If people came to believe most others would be fair, coverage of found property being returned to its owner should increase.
If trust in others declined, coverage should shift from accounts of people trusting others without safeguards to accounts of people being shortchanged or overcharged.
In neighborhood life, if people became more willing to trust neighbors, coverage should shift from suspicion of newcomers toward neighborly sharing and welcome.
If people increasingly assumed others would act fairly, coverage of unprompted generosity toward strangers should become more common.
Coverage of people feeling trapped, demoralised, or without hope should rise if overall life satisfaction fell.
Coverage of live entertainment returning at full capacity should rise if life satisfaction improved, since leisure reopening signals a better mood.
Language of dread and uncertainty about the future should give way to language of upbeat, cheerful outlook if satisfaction moved toward Satisfied.
In coverage of social care, reports of care being secured and waits cut should be replaced by reports of closures and unmet need if satisfaction moved toward Dissatisfied.
Coverage of loneliness among older people and people living alone should rise if life satisfaction fell.
Public discourse increasingly describes standardized, uniform approaches as desirable, suggesting a shift away from valuing individual creative expression.
Coverage of classrooms increasingly emphasizes measurable outcomes and accountability metrics over open-ended learning, consistent with less emphasis on creativity.
Descriptions of admirable personal qualities shift from unconventional, visionary traits toward dependable, rule-abiding traits.
Coverage of music shifts from celebrating original songwriting and experimentation toward cover acts, tributes, and playlist-driven listening.
Marketing coverage increasingly stresses testing and data over bold, original campaign ideas, suggesting less emphasis on creativity.
Coverage of identity theft committed by relatives rises over time, reflecting more reported distrust of family members.

If the average answer moved toward 'Strongly disagree', coverage of formal affirmative-action measures for women in admissions should rise, because such measures signal public acceptance that women's university access is a legitimate policy goal.

If the average answer moved toward 'Strongly disagree', reporting on professional-school admissions should increasingly highlight women applicants and record female intake, reflecting a shift toward treating women's higher education as normal.

If the average answer moved toward 'Agree strongly', coverage should shift from framing family support as shared between children to framing sons as the expected source of parental security, reflecting a stronger gender-differentiated view of who should be educated and supported.

If the average answer moved toward 'Agree strongly', references to sons as old-age security and the family's need for a male heir in advisory or opinion coverage should increase, signalling renewed emphasis on investing in boys' futures.

Coverage of national productivity stagnation and falling workforce participation will rise, signalling growing public concern that reduced emphasis on work threatens living standards (a shift toward viewing it as a bad thing).
Coverage of unpaid care will increasingly frame reduced paid work as a positive route to caring for family, reflecting more favourable attitudes toward working less.
Commentary shifting from valuing employment as a source of contribution and self-reliance toward describing idleness and drift will indicate a move toward seeing less work as a bad thing.
Discussion of weekend and holiday time moving from shop-hours and trading rules toward personal boundaries and switching off after hours will signal growing approval of less time spent working.
Coverage of shorter working weeks and time poverty will increase as the framing of reduced hours as a desirable goal becomes more common, indicating attitudes moving toward a good thing.
Coverage of technology development increasingly uses investment and talent-pipeline language, which would track a more positive public framing of technological progress (Direction B).
Local-impact complaints about data centers rise over time, reflecting growing public resistance to technology buildout (Direction A).
Early coverage frames technology in visionary, aspirational terms, while later coverage shifts to words suggesting overreach and loss of public control (Direction A).

Commercial spaceflight coverage moves from skeptical framing about wasted spending toward celebration of reusable rockets and record launches, indicating a more favorable view of technology development (Direction B).
Coverage of solar and wind power increasingly emphasizes cost savings and deployment records, reflecting a more positive attitude toward technological development (Direction B).
Coverage of petition fatigue and burnout rises over time, as people report tiring of being asked to sign things and the average answer moves toward 'Not done'.

Coverage shifts from paper-based petition collection, where forms are posted or returned by mail, toward link-based signing that is shared and completed in one step. This reflects a rise in signing and an answer moving toward 'Have done'.
Animal welfare and environmental campaigns increasingly ask for a signature to push a specific ban, and coverage of these campaigns grows, pointing toward more people having signed.

In political coverage, petitions move from being described as record-setting or massive events to being described as one more petition in a crowded field, consistent with a decline in signing and an answer moving toward 'Not done'.
Milestone language about signature counts becomes more common as online campaigns grow, indicating more people signing and an answer moving toward 'Have done'.
As boycott fatigue sets in, coverage increasingly describes the public as tired of or overwhelmed by boycott calls, which should track a drift toward 'Would never do'.

Coverage of consumer brands drawn into political controversy should increasingly report named boycott participation and customer defections, consistent with a rise in people who have actually boycotted.
Early coverage frames boycott refusal as a firm personal principle, while later coverage shifts to people reporting they have already stopped buying, reflecting movement toward 'Have done'.
On energy and fuel companies, early coverage features pledges to skip their products, while later coverage features people calling boycotts pointless, reflecting movement toward 'Would never do'.
Reporting on formal boycott lists and pledge signers should rise as more individuals personally commit to boycotting, pointing toward 'Have done'.

Coverage of boycotts framed as ineffective or failed rises when people are reporting fewer boycott actions, so explicit skepticism about boycotts should increase in the period where participation falls.
Reports naming specific corporate boycotts of major brands should increase when people are actively joining boycotts, since named-brand campaigns are what drive participation.

Within coverage of political and geopolitical disputes, mentions of boycott calls should increase as more people report joining them, and boycott-related language about ending or lifting campaigns should decline.

Early-stage boycott coverage describing people who merely heard of or considered boycotts should shift toward later coverage describing people who have sustained boycotts over time, indicating movement toward reported participation.
In retail coverage, early reports of boycott days and pledge signers should give way to later reports of shoppers returning to the same retailers, reflecting a move toward reported non-participation.

Commentary describing class barriers as structural and fixed (a 'glass floor' or 'class ceiling', or wealth passed down as an advantage) becomes more common, signaling a shift toward the view that luck and birth determine outcomes more than effort.

Coverage that frames effort as the reliable path to security (rebuilding after setbacks, slow compounding payoff) becomes more frequent, signaling a shift toward the view that hard work leads to a better life in the long run.
Among coverage of tech and coding careers, stories crediting skill-based self-training with landing good jobs increase, signaling a shift toward the view that effort and skill are rewarded.

Over time, descriptions of setbacks shift from individual failure framed as final (losing everything) toward accounts of recovery through persistence, signaling movement toward the view that hard work pays off.

In coverage of manufacturing and rural workers, the explanation for job security shifts from personal merit and steady pride toward outside forces such as plant closures and outsourcing, signaling movement toward the view that luck and circumstance decide outcomes.
Confidence in the Civil Service fell (Direction A) as coverage of public-sector industrial action and union disputes grew, since strikes and ballots signal discontent with the institution.
Confidence rose (Direction B) as coverage of civil service graduate and apprenticeship schemes reported strong demand and filled places, signalling a healthier, more attractive institution.
Confidence fell (Direction A) as framing shifted from the civil service as a neutral, constitutional body to a partisan 'blob' accused of undermining elected governments.
Confidence rose (Direction B) as coverage of government digital and benefits services moved from reporting delays and system failures to reporting delivery milestones.
Coverage of women's organizations increasingly centers on regulatory scrutiny of their tax status and finances, which should erode public confidence and push the average answer toward 'None at all'.

Early coverage describes women's organizations mainly through self-reported activity, while later coverage relies on independent third-party ratings and audits, which should signal rising confidence toward 'A great deal'.
Women's service clubs receiving high ratings from charity evaluators should increase over time, signaling growing confidence toward 'A great deal'.
Coverage of women's shelters shifts from routine service announcements to legal disputes and closures, which should move the average answer toward 'None at all'.
Reporting on surging demand and donations to women's support groups should increase over time, reflecting stronger public trust and a shift toward 'A great deal'.
Coverage of enforceable labor and environmental commitments in the revised pact rises over time, reflecting a shift toward favorable framing of the agreement and higher public confidence.
Within coverage of the North American trade pact, descriptions of the agreement as enforceable and well-crafted become more common as confidence in it rises.
Early coverage describes the agreement with crisis and disaster vocabulary, while later coverage shifts to stability and implementation language, consistent with rising confidence.
Coverage of Canada's role in the trade pact moves from retaliation and protectionism framing toward cooperation and completed-deal framing as confidence rises.
Coverage emphasizing escalating trade-war measures and retaliation grows over time, reflecting a shift toward distrust of the trade relationship and lower confidence.
Coverage of politically active 'dark money' nonprofits rises over time, which would erode public confidence in charitable organizations generally (Direction A).
Coverage of large philanthropic foundations and their pledges grows over time, reflecting rising public enthusiasm for giving (Direction B).
Coverage shifts from traditional relief-distribution language toward grassroots mutual-aid language, indicating a rise in favorable framing of charitable activity (Direction B).
Within coverage of national food-aid networks, reporting shifts from praise of efficient operations to complaints about overpaid leadership, signaling declining confidence (Direction A).
Reports of cryptocurrency-based charity scams become more frequent over time, adding a new fraud vector that undermines trust in charities (Direction A).

Coverage increasingly frames expert-led decision-making as detached from ordinary people, so the share of articles using anti-establishment distance language rises as opinion shifts toward 'Very bad'.
As opinion moves toward 'Very good', coverage uses more language praising professional competence and specialist qualification in public decision-making.
Within coverage of independent economic forecasting bodies, credibility language rises as public attitudes toward expert rule move toward 'Very good'.
Early coverage presents experts as offering advice that politicians weigh, while later coverage describes experts as taking over decisions, tracking a shift toward 'Very bad'.
In Brexit coverage, early references to experts warning about outcomes shift to dismissive 'Project Fear' framing that rejects expert judgement, consistent with movement toward 'Very bad'.
Coverage of minimally invasive and digitally enabled medical care rises over time, reflecting growing public experience of health technology making care easier and less burdensome (direction A).
Coverage of chemical and plastic contamination grows over time, as concern about harms from industrial products increases and undermines confidence that technology improves health (direction B).

Coverage shifts from describing pre-modern threats (epidemics, famine, smog) toward describing modern provisions (clean water, electrified homes, eradicated diseases), signaling growing belief that science improves daily life (direction A).

In coverage of technology in schools, early enthusiasm for digital learning tools gives way to concern about screens and learning loss, reflecting a move toward skepticism that technology makes life better (direction B).

Coverage of digital harms and security failures rises over time, as public attention to deepfakes, breaches, and surveillance tools grows and erodes belief that technology makes life easier (direction B).

Coverage of tangible clean-tech and energy-storage deployments rises over time, reflecting growing public visibility of concrete technological gains that could support optimism about future opportunities.
Coverage of tech-sector hiring contraction and graduate job scarcity rises over time, signaling growing pessimism that technology is narrowing rather than widening opportunities for newcomers.

Among coverage of young people, mentions of accessible tech pathways such as short-form training and apprenticeships increase over time, reflecting a belief that science and technology open routes for the next generation.

Over time, coverage shifts from abstract future-oriented technological imagery toward concrete affordability and cost pressures facing young adults, indicating a move toward pessimism about future opportunities.

In coverage of research universities and labs, reports of funding cuts and closures give way over time to reports of new facilities and major grants, indicating renewed confidence in science as a source of future opportunity.
Coverage of people abandoning an activity will rise in frequency, using idioms of quitting that differ from earlier 'stopped/gave up' phrasing, so the average answer shifts toward 'Not done'.

Reports of people trying cold-water or open-water activities for the first time will become more common, indicating more respondents have done a new activity, so the average shifts toward 'Have done'.

In coverage of personal goal lists, the language shifts from completing items to deferring them indefinitely, so the average answer moves toward 'Not done'.
Mentions of people shelving leisure or social plans for lack of interest, rather than lack of time, will become more prevalent, consistent with a shift toward 'Not done'.

Coverage of electoral reform and voter access increases over time. This signals growing public emphasis on elections as the means of choosing leaders, which should move the essentialness rating toward 'essential characteristic' (Direction A).
Anti-democratic sentiment framed as technocratic or expert rule rises over time. Acceptance that elections are dispensable should shift the rating toward 'against democracy' (Direction B).
Discourse shifts from pro-election vocabulary to anti-election, expert-rule vocabulary. This contrast indicates movement toward 'against democracy' (Direction B).

On the topic of upper chambers and legislative seats, coverage shifts from appointed or hereditary seating toward directly elected members. This reflects a move toward treating voter selection as essential (Direction A).

Growing popularity of structured mindfulness and reflective self-help practices signals rising personal contemplation of life's meaning, so these brand names and practice terms should increase in coverage.
If leisure shifts from reflective pursuits toward passive entertainment, coverage of streaming and reality-TV viewing should displace coverage of contemplative reading and discussion.
Rising attention to palliative care and terminal illness reflects heightened engagement with life review and legacy, so reflective end-of-life language should increase.
A move toward purposeful, intentional travel over cheap, escapist holidays signals more reflective life orientation, so pilgrimage-style vocabulary should replace all-inclusive leisure vocabulary.

If people think less about life's deeper questions and more about immediate consumption, coverage of impulse shopping trends such as fast fashion hauls should rise alongside distraction-driven purchasing language.

Coverage of people who identify as unbelievers or who are outside church life becomes more frequent, using terms that name a non-religious identity rather than the generic 'no religion' or 'nones' labels already tested.
Life-event framing shifts from church-based ceremonies to secular alternatives. Earlier coverage centres on church-based family rituals, and later coverage centres on humanist and civil ceremonies.
Within religious education and school worship, coverage moves from compulsory, universal worship to opt-outs and secular curricula, which signals a decline in routine religious participation.
Frequent religious participation grows through online channels, so coverage of online and livestreamed congregations increases as a sign of more regular worship.
Sabbath and Lord's Day observance is described as abandoned more often, which tracks a move toward never attending.

Public discussion of bribery increasingly invokes structural integrity safeguards (open contracting, beneficial ownership, lobbying registers). Stronger rejection of bribe-taking should show up as more of this institutional vocabulary, so the average answer moves toward 'Never justifiable'.

Coverage of traffic enforcement increasingly describes cash payments to officers as a normal shortcut. If people treat these payments as acceptable, the average answer moves toward 'Always justifiable'.

Early coverage frames bribe-taking as a casual thank-you or a small informal perk. Later coverage frames it as betrayal of the public and rot in institutions. Hardening attitudes move the average toward 'Never justifiable'.

For public-service workers such as teachers and social workers, early coverage treats accepting money from clients as a plain crime. Later coverage treats it as an understandable response to underpayment. Growing sympathy moves the average toward 'Always justifiable'.

Commentary that minimises bribery as a minor matter of convenience (grey area, not a big deal, a bit of extra) becomes more common. Growing normalisation moves the average toward 'Always justifiable'.
Public acceptance of divorce grew as talk of being trapped in a marriage and of divorce as a personal decision became more common, pushing the average toward 'Always justifiable'.
Coverage of domestic abuse increasingly framed leaving an abusive spouse as justified, which would move attitudes toward 'Always justifiable'.
Rising alarm about a culture of divorce and eroding marital vows would signal a shift toward 'Never justifiable'.
Discourse moved from tolerance of personal choice toward moral-decline framing of divorce, consistent with a shift toward 'Never justifiable'.
Among coverage of divorced women, shame-based language gave way to language of self-reliance, consistent with a shift toward 'Always justifiable'.

Coverage of wife-beating attitudes shifts toward explicit condemnation of hitting women, so reporting on 'hitting a woman' and 'striking a wife' as unacceptable should rise, indicating movement toward 'Never justifiable'.
Justifications of spousal violence framed as crimes of passion or provocation become more common in reporting, indicating movement toward 'Always justifiable'.

Campaigns against gender violence, such as the White Ribbon and 16 Days of Activism, increase in coverage with explicit language that wife beating is unacceptable, indicating movement toward 'Never justifiable'.
Reporting moves from a culture of silence and hushing up abuse toward survivors speaking out and public naming of abusers, indicating movement toward 'Never justifiable'.

In Demographic and Health Survey coverage, language shifts from calling wife beating wrong toward framing it as justified by wifely disobedience or neglect, indicating movement toward 'Always justifiable'.
Coverage of online fraud and impersonation rises over time, reflecting growing wariness toward strangers and a shift toward distrust of others (Direction A).
Coverage of formal verification and vetting systems rises over time, reflecting greater reliance on institutional checks rather than personal trust in strangers (Direction B).
Within coverage of schools and children's activities, references to safeguarding and stranger precautions increase over time, signalling reduced trust in other adults (Direction A).
Coverage shifts from language about being cheated by others toward language about trusted, endorsed people, indicating rising trust in others (Direction B).
In online marketplace coverage, language about in-person handshake dealings gives way to language about scams and fake listings, indicating declining trust in other people (Direction A).
Coverage of gated communities, private security, and residential surveillance rises over time, reflecting growing wariness toward unfamiliar people, so distrust of strangers increases (Direction A).
Discussion of neighborhood social apps and community forums increasingly centers on warnings about unfamiliar people, so distrust of strangers increases (Direction A).
Reporting on social trust research, trust surveys, and efforts to rebuild interpersonal trust increases over time, reflecting a rise in general trust in others (Direction B).
Descriptions of neighborhood life shift from open, informal sociability toward guarded, closed-off routines, so distrust of strangers grows (Direction A).
Coverage of ride-hailing and home-rental platforms shifts from safety-anxious framing toward confident, trusting framing, so trust in strangers increases (Direction B).

Coverage of birthright citizenship and children born to immigrant mothers rises over time, so mentions of immigrant-mother births should increase, pointing toward more respondents reporting an immigrant mother (Yes).

Among coverage of Latino and Mexican-American families, references to deep family roots in the U.S. should grow over time, reflecting more multigenerational, native-born mothers and a shift toward No.

Coverage shifts from exclusion-era immigration rules (quotas and national-origin limits) toward family-sponsorship and parent-of-citizen provisions, which concern immigrant mothers and so suggest a move toward Yes.
In maternal health coverage, early references to immigrant mothers lacking coverage give way to later references to U.S.-born babies and citizen children, suggesting a drift toward No.

Reporting on the path from temporary status to permanent residence grows over time, so references to green card holders and lawful permanent residents increase, consistent with more immigrant mothers (Yes).
